explanations.explanation: Isaiah says they speak "With pride and arrogance of heart…" (Isa 9:9). Their city has taken a hit, and they answer with a building upgrade. Friend, I once told a cookie that it was my best work while it sat there burnt on one side, so I know that kind of talk. Isaiah just names it plainly.

Isaiah doesn't say sorrow anywhere in this verse. He says they speak with "…pride and arrogance of heart…" Listen to the words he gives them: "…we will rebuild with finished stone…" That's a plan being announced, friend, and the word Isaiah picks is pride.

Fear isn't what Isaiah names. He says they speak with "…pride and arrogance of heart…" Their words are "…we will rebuild with finished stone…" and "…we will replace them with cedars." Nobody in that speech sounds nervous, baker. They sound like folks who just won a home makeover.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "Aram from the east and Philistia from the west have devoured Israel with open mouths." That's one nation on each side, and Philistia is the one on the west. So Philistia is your answer. I think this is a heavy picture, and Isaiah gives it to us plainly.

Isaiah doesn't name Egypt in this verse. He says "Aram from the east and Philistia from the west…" Philistia is the one on the west side. Egypt is a big name, friend, so I get why it jumped out at you.

Moab isn't in this verse, baker. Isaiah says "Aram from the east and Philistia from the west have devoured Israel with open mouths." So the western side belongs to Philistia. Moab will have to wait for another passage.

That's the opposite of what Isaiah says, friend. Right after Aram and Philistia devour Israel, he says, "Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised." The anger is still there. It's the kind of line you read twice to make sure it says what you think it says, and this one does.

Right, baker. Isaiah says, "Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised." (Isa 9:12). Aram and Philistia have already come with open mouths, and the anger hasn't turned away. "Despite all this…" is Isaiah's way of saying there's more still to come in this passage.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "…the people did not return to Him who struck them; they did not seek the LORD of Hosts." They got struck, and they still didn't turn back or go looking for Him. Two lines, friend, and both say they didn't.

Not quite, friend. Isaiah says, "…the people did not return to Him who struck them; they did not seek the LORD of Hosts." So they did not return. It's easy to read right past a little word like "not," and I've done it with a recipe. It never ends well for the dough.

That's it, baker. Isaiah says the head is the elder and honorable man, and "…the tail is the prophet who teaches lies." I think a prophet who teaches lies is a hard thing to read about. The verse names both parts of the picture, so nobody has to guess.

Isaiah doesn't name a king here, friend. He says the head is the elder and honorable man, and the tail is "…the prophet who teaches lies." A king would make a good guess, I admit. But I'll stick with what the verse says, and it says prophet.

No priest or bribe shows up in this verse, baker. Isaiah says the head is the elder and honorable man, and the tail is "…the prophet who teaches lies." The verse is short and it only names those two. If I added a priest, I'd be putting extra sprinkles on a cookie that didn't ask for them.

Yes, friend. Isaiah says, "For those who guide this people mislead them…" Then he adds that "…those they mislead are swallowed up." That's a guide leading people the wrong way. It's like following a map to the bakery and ending up at a parking lot, except this one is far more serious.
Protect isn't the word, baker. Isaiah says, "For those who guide this people mislead them…" Notice what happens next: "…those they mislead are swallowed up."

Isaiah doesn't say comfort, friend. He says, "For those who guide this people mislead them…" Comfort is what a good guide gives. These guides lead people off the path instead, and the verse says the misled are swallowed up.

explanations.answer: Every one of them is godless and wicked
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "For every one of them is godless and wicked, and every mouth speaks folly." That's the reason the verse gives, and it covers the young men, the fatherless and the widows. I won't add any reasons of my own to it.

explanations.answer: They refused to leave the land
explanations.explanation: Leaving the land never comes up in this verse, friend. Isaiah gives the reason himself: "For every one of them is godless and wicked, and every mouth speaks folly." So the answer is what he says about them, not where they stood. When Isaiah gives a reason, I just read it out.

explanations.answer: They bowed down to Aram's gods
explanations.explanation: Aram's gods aren't mentioned here, baker. Aram is only named earlier as a nation that came against Israel (Isa 9:12). The reason in this verse is that "…every one of them is godless and wicked, and every mouth speaks folly." That's the whole answer, and I'm not putting words in it that aren't there.

Yes, friend. Isaiah says, "By the wrath of the LORD of Hosts the land is scorched, and the people are fuel for the fire." It's a heavy verse and I won't joke over it. Wrath is the word the text uses, and I'll leave it at that.

Mercy isn't the word here, baker. Isaiah says, "By the wrath of the LORD of Hosts the land is scorched…" A scorched land and mercy don't fit in the same sentence of this verse. The word Isaiah picks is wrath.

Patience isn't what Isaiah says, friend. He says, "By the wrath of the LORD of Hosts the land is scorched…" Wrath is the word he picks, and it goes with the fire he's been describing. I'll leave the verse the way he wrote it.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says, "They carve out what is on the right, but they are still hungry; they eat what is on the left, but they are still not satisfied." They keep eating and they are still hungry. I think that's a heavy line, so I'll let it stand.

Thankful isn't in this verse, friend. Isaiah says, "…they are still hungry…" and "…still not satisfied." They carve and they eat, and they still come up empty. Thankful would be a nicer picture, but it isn't the one he paints.

Generous isn't the word, baker. Isaiah says, "…they are still hungry; they eat what is on the left, but they are still not satisfied." The verse is all about eating without ever being full. Nothing in it shows anybody giving anything away.

Yes, friend. Isaiah says, "Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; together they turn against Judah." Judah is the one they turn against together. So Judah is your answer. It's a rough picture, and Isaiah doesn't soften it.
Egypt isn't in this verse, baker. Isaiah says, "Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; together they turn against Judah." Egypt is a famous name, but the name the verse gives is Judah.

Moab doesn't appear in this verse, friend. Isaiah says, "Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; together they turn against Judah." The two tribes turn on Judah together. So Judah is the name the verse gives.

Yes, baker. Isaiah says those laws are made "…to deprive the poor of fair treatment and withhold justice from the oppressed of My people…" These are the unjust statutes and oppressive decrees he just named (Isa 10:1), and the poor and the oppressed are who they're aimed at. It's a serious thing, so I'll just say it plainly.
The verse says poor, friend. Isaiah says the laws are made "…to deprive the poor of fair treatment…" Rich isn't the word he uses. The ones kept from fair treatment are the poor.

Strong isn't the word, baker. Isaiah says the laws are made "…to deprive the poor of fair treatment and withhold justice from the oppressed of My people…" The people named there are the poor and the oppressed. That's who the verse points to.
Yes, friend. Isaiah says they do it "…to make widows their prey and orphans their plunder." I think this one hurts. The text names widows and orphans, and I'll stay quiet and let the words stand.

Not quite, baker. Isaiah does say it: "…to make widows their prey and orphans their plunder." I think this is one of the harder lines in the whole passage. It's also exactly what the text says, so I won't soften it.

That's it, baker. Isaiah asks, "To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth?" and he leaves no answer in the verse. I think that empty space is the point. A question with no helper in it is a heavy thing to hear.

No allies show up in the verse, friend. Isaiah asks, "To whom will you flee for help?" and never names anyone who will answer. The very next verse says, "Nothing will remain but to crouch among the captives or fall among the slain." (Isa 10:4) I think the question is there to show no helper is coming.

explanations.answer: Their wealth will buy them time
explanations.explanation: Isaiah doesn't say that, baker. He asks, "Where will you leave your wealth?" and gives no spot where it stays safe. Then the verse after it says "Nothing will remain…" but captivity or death (Isa 10:4). So the wealth doesn't buy anything in this picture.

Yes, friend. Isaiah says, "Nothing will remain but to crouch among the captives or fall among the slain." Those are the only two things he lists. It's the hardest line in this stretch, so I'll say it plainly and leave it there.

Hiding and begging aren't in the verse, baker. Isaiah says, "Nothing will remain but to crouch among the captives or fall among the slain." The two things are captivity and death. It's a heavy verse, and I won't add anything to it.

The verse doesn't say poverty or shame, friend. Isaiah says, "Nothing will remain but to crouch among the captives or fall among the slain." That means being taken captive or dying. It's a hard thing to read, and I'd rather give you the exact words than a softer guess.
